en: Viktor; Russian astronomer who proposed the planetesimal hypothesis for how the Solar System formed from a disk of gas and dust around the Sun (1917-1999).

Michael J. S.; British astronomer who in 2002 chaired the first Planetary Science Decadal Survey, which established NASA’s New Frontiers Program, including the New Horizons mission to Pluto and the Kuiper Belt (1934-2018).
Robert S.; American astronomer at the US Naval Observatory who is considered the co-discoverer of Charon and was the first to calculate the Pluto system’s mass (1942-1993).
Shafika Gil’mievna; Soviet astronomer of Tatar origin, celestial mechanics expert who developed an analytical theory for Pluto’s motion and derived new orbital elements (1915-2002).
Ernest Clare; American astronomer who calculated one of the first independent orbits of Pluto, shortly after that planet’s 1930 discovery by Lowell Observatory’s Clyde Tombaugh (1890-1964).

Paolo; Italian planetary scientist who conducted critical investigations of the formation and collisional evolution of small bodies, satellites, and space debris, including Kuiper Belt objects (1953-2000).
First Japanese spacecraft to the Moon, 1990.
A series of seven unmanned U.S. probes to the lunar surface, 1966-1968.
A series of eight unmanned Soviet lunar and interplanetary probes, 1964–1970.
A series of Indian lunar probes, beginning in 2008.
A series of 24 unmanned Soviet lunar probes launched between 1959 and 1976.
A series of Chinese lunar probes, beginning in 2013.
William C.; Original Science Payload Manager of the New Horizons mission to Pluto and the Kuiper Belt (1945-2017).
Percival; American astronomer who in 1906-1916 undertook extensive searches of transneptunian planets (1855-1916).
Henry L.; astronomer at Lowell Observatory, who obtained early photographic plates that remain critical to determination of Pluto’s orbit (1910-2007).
Bishun; Indian-born American atmosphere chemistry scientist, investigated, in particular, tholins, the organic molecules that probably account for the darkest regions on Pluto (1933–2013).
Jeanne Baret (Baré); first woman to have completed circumnavigation voyage of the globe (1740-1807).

Orville (1871–1948) and Wilbur (1867–1912), brothers, U.S. aviation pioneers who invented, built, and flew in 1903 the world’s first successful powered heavier-than-air flying machine (airplane) with a pilot aboard.
Rolan; Georgian (Caucasus) astronomer. Investigated the dynamics, astrometry and photometry of Pluto (1931–2010).

Ahmed Muhiddin, also known as Piri Reis, Ottoman navigator and cartographer (c. 1470–1553). Author of one of the earliest existing world maps in 1513. His “Book of the Sea” (1521), containing 290 maps, was one of the most famous cartographical work
Auguste; Swiss-Belgian inventor and physicist known for his pioneering balloon flights into the Earth’s upper atmosphere up to 17 km (1884–1962).

Antonio; Italian scholar and explorer, whose journal is the only original description of the discoveries made during the first circumnavigation of the Earth which started in Spain in 1519 under the leadership of Magellan (c.1491 – c.1531).
Juan Sebastián; Spanish explorer of Basque origin, who completed in 1522 the first circumnavigation of the Earth which started in 1519 under the leadership of Magellan (c.1476–1526).

Series of the Soviet Union’s 16 spacecraft sent to Venus in 1961–1983. The missions accomplished a number of firsts, including the first human made device to enter the atmosphere of another planet (Venera 3, 1966), to measure in situ atmosphere compo
One of the Hero Twins (with Xbalanque) in Mayan mythology, who defeated the lords of the Underworld in a ball game.
Nyanga (Eastern Dem. Rep. Congo/Zaire) epic hero who travelled to the underworld and after returning home became a wise and powerful king.

A pair of the Soviet Union’s Vega 1 and Vega 2 spacecraft launched in 1984 that were the first ones to fly balloons on another planet (Venus, 1985) and then the first ones to image the nucleus of a comet (1P/Halley, 1986).
A bottomless lake, one of the entrances to the underworld in Greek mythology.
Damon; American astronomer; investigated the formation history of Pluto (1959–2004).

Epic hero of the Chochenyo/Ohlone (N. California) mythology, an anthropomorphic being resembling a peregrine falcon, who traveled to the underworld to battle Wiwe (“Body of Stone”), the lord of the underworld.
Edmund; New Zealand mountaineer (1919–2008).
Son of Odin, who rode the horse Sleipnir into the underworld to retrieve his brother, Balder.
Junko Tabei, Japanese mountaineer and the first woman to climb both Mount Everest and the Seven Summits (1939–2016).
Thomas Boyd; American mechanical/space engineer, first project manager of the New Horizons mission to Pluto and the Kuiper Belt (1941–2014).
Zulu tale hero, who followed a porcupine underground and came upon the village of dead souls.
Korean traveler and scholar, who crossed the Asian continent from China to Arabia and back (724-727), and documented the journey in his journals (704–787).
Robert H.; American astronomer, co-discoverer (1955) of Pluto’s 6.4-day rotation period (1923–1989).
Ash-Sharīf al-Idrīsī; Arabian mapmaker and geographer (1100–1165/66).
An Icelandic volcano believed to be the entrance to Hell in medieval European times.
First fully operational US space shuttle, launched first on April 12, 1981, and lost during re-entry on February 1, 2003.
Lisa; Led the development of the RALPH instrument, the visual and infrared imager and spectrometer on the New Horizons spacecraft (1966-2017).
Carl; German physicist, inventor of the blink comparator which Clyde Tombaugh used for discovery of Pluto (1858-1927).
Francesco; Italian astronomer who carried out early studies of the orbit of Pluto (1900-1976).
Kenneth; Irish astronomer, the first to propose the existence of a disk of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune, now known as the Edgeworth-Kuiper Belt (1880-1972).
Jan Hendrik, Dutch astronomer, first described the Oort Cloud, a theoretical cloud of icy planetesimals beyond the Kuiper Belt, and believed to be the source of long- period comets (1900 to 1992).
In The Inferno by Dante, Beatrice descends into hell to find Virgil and ask him to guide Dante. She later guides Dante through Paradise in Paradiso.
Inanna was the Queen of Heaven in ancient Sumerian mythology. She visited the Underworld but was permitted to return in exchange for the life of her husband, Dumuzi.
In ancient Sumerian mythology, Dumuzi was a god of the harvest. He was taken down into the Underworld, but permitted to return to earth for half of each year, resulting in the cycle of the seasons.
Zheng He, Chinese explorer, led voyages of Asia, Africa, and the Middle East (1371 to 1433).
A series of US space probes sent to the Moon during 1961-1965. In 1964, Ranger 7 obtained the first close-up images of an extraterrestrial surface.
Early US lunar, planetary, and heliospheric missions including the first to Jupiter and Saturn, 1958-1997.
A pair of US-launched Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft that performed the “grand tour” of all four giant planets (1977-1989).
Two Soviet Union planetary rovers that were sent to the surface of the Moon (1970, 1973). Lunokhod 1 was the first remote-controlled, wheeled robot to land on and rove on an extraterrestrial body.
Tenzing Norgay; Nepalese (Sherpa) mountaineer (1914–1986).
Underworld in Inuit myths.
US Mars orbiter and landed missions that conducted the first successful explorations of the surface of Mars, 1976 to 1982.
James; American astronomer, discoverer of the atmosphere of Pluto (1943–2011).
Clyde William; American astronomer, discoverer of Pluto (1906–1997).
Italian; Dante’s guide through Hell and Purgatory in the Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri (1265–1321).
Elizabeth “Bessie”; early American aviator and the first woman of African-American and Native American descent to earn a pilot’s license (1892-1926).
Sally; American physicist, astronaut, and first American woman in space (1951-2012).
Ancestral beings in Yolngu (Australia) myth who traveled between the island of the dead and Australia.
Venetia; British schoolgirl, who suggested in 1930 the name “Pluto” for Tombaugh’s newly discovered planet (1918–2009).
The deepest, darkest pit of the Underworld in Greek mythology.
Japanese Hayabusa (literally Peregrine Falcon) spacecraft that performed the first asteroid sample return (2003–2010).
A powerful, eight-legged horse in Norse mythology who carried Odin into the Underworld.
Soviet Union's Sputnik 1 (literally Satellite 1), the first human-built satellite of the Earth (1957).
Väinämöinen is a central character of the Finnish national epic The Kalevala. He traveled to the Underworld to seek knowledge of the dead.
Lemminkäinen is a hero of the Finnish national epic The Kalevala. He travels to the Underworld to capture the black swan.
Rosetta mission, the first mission to orbit and land a spacecraft on a comet.
Charles T.; American astronomer and discoverer of 2060 Chiron (1940-2011).
Angioletta; Italian planetary scientist (1946-2011).
Second fully operational US Space Shuttle, first launched on April 4, 1983. It was lost during its tenth launch on January 28, 1986.
